newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Shell output cut, staff held in Nigeria row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Shell output cut, staff held in Nigeria row.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell said on Monday it had been dragged into a dispute between villagers in Nigeria's oil-rich Niger delta region and 126 of its staff and contractors, all Nigerians, had been detained.
The trouble began at the weekend when rival community groups occupied several installations, forcing a cut in crude production. Exports were not affected for the time being, the company said.

A dispute over the relocation of the Warri southwest local government headquarters escalated on Saturday when community groups overran six of Shell's pumping stations in the northern swamp area west of the river Niger.
Shell said the 126 detained employees and contractors were being detained by community groups who invaded the stations at Egwa, Odidi, Batan and Jones Creek.
Six staff injured in the attack had received first aid and were in a stable condition, Shell said, and some computers and telephones had been damaged during the occupation.
"At present the situation is quiet and the company believes all staff and contractor staff are safe," Shell said in a statement issued in London.
The occupation of the flow stations forced Shell to shut in some 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil production, equivalent to about 10 percent of its Nigerian output.
But exports and deliveries to refineries in Nigeria had not been affected and would continue as normal for the foreseeable future.
"This will not affect exports for the rest of this month," said a Shell official.
Oil markets were unmoved, world benchmark Brent Blend crude oil trading down 25 cents at $19.74 a barrel, but Shell's shares were rattled.
Shell Transport and Trading shed 1.85 percent, against a 0.67 percent fall in the value of the FTSE 100 index.
Shell Nigeria's Western Division, where the flow stations have been shut in, normally produces about 450,000 bpd.
Nigeria, with output of about 2.15 million bpd is the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC)'s fifth biggest producer. Shell pumps about half of that.
Community disturbances and sabotage have hit Shell's Nigerian operations in the past but increased community spending had reduced the losses in recent years.
Acts of sabotage in protest at the company's environmental record led Shell to withdraw from the Niger delta's Ogoniland in 1993 and it has still to return.
In 1994, Shell Western Division headquarters in Warri were surrounded by local protestors seeking greater benefits from oil output in their region.
Shell said it had passed on a list of demands to the local authorities at the request of the villagers but had not asked the Nigerian government for any assistance.
"We need to re-establish dialogue with the local communities," said a spokesman in London.
